Turf beside a Windermere pool cage or lanai

Turf around a pool or inside a screen enclosure prices at the residential range, $8–$18 per square foot as of September 2026. On a Windermere lakefront lot, the pool deck and the state's 10-foot waterbody setback frequently sit close enough together that both get measured on the same visit.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Say you have a 400 sq ft strip between a Windermere pool cage and Lake Down

A 400 sq ft strip of turf between a screened pool cage and a Lake Down shoreline, with an existing seawall running the property line, prices at $8–$18 per square foot, or about $3,200 to $7,200 at the published range, glued at the deck edge and pinned along the outer perimeter. Because the seawall already separates the yard from open water, the state's 10-foot setback doesn't reduce the usable strip the way it would on an unwalled shoreline.

Without a seawall, the same 400 sq ft strip would need roughly the first 10 feet from the water's edge left as-is, cutting the turfed area down before the per-square-foot math even starts.

When the pool cage meets the lake setback

A screened pool on an in-town lake lot, or on a golf-community lot backing up to one of the Butler Chain's connecting canals, sometimes leaves only a narrow strip of ground between the cage and the water. That strip is exactly where the state’s 10-foot waterbody buffer applies, seawall exception included, so measuring the pool deck and the shoreline distance on the same visit avoids planning turf for a strip that isn't available to use.

Where a seawall already runs the property line, which is common on older in-town lake lots, the setback doesn't apply, and turf can run to the wall itself.

Why a pool quote often carries two separate turf line items

A Windermere property getting both a glued lanai floor and an open deck border should see those priced as two distinct line items on the same quote rather than one blended per-square-foot number, since the underlay, adhesive, and labor for a glued slab application cost differently than rock, compaction, and staked edges for an open border. A homeowner comparing two quotes for the same combined project should check that both bids split the work the same way; a quote that bundles everything into one number makes it harder to tell which area is driving most of the cost.

Turf inside the screen, glued rather than pinned

Turf laid over a pool deck's existing concrete or pavers inside a screen enclosure gets glued down at the edges rather than staked, since there's no soil underneath to anchor a perimeter nail into. A drainage underlay goes between the concrete and the turf backing so water from a rinse or a storm has somewhere to go besides sitting on the slab, which matters more in a screened, lower-airflow space than it would in an open yard.

What actually holds up a turf ribbon between pavers?

A narrow strip of turf set into a paver joint near the pool does not sit on a rock base at all; the pavers themselves carry the load, and the turf gets a thin leveling layer of sand in the joint rather than the two to four inches used everywhere else on a Windermere lot. That thin joint still has to drain rather than trap water against the paver edges, so the sand underneath needs to stay loose enough to percolate, the same principle behind leaving native soil uncompacted under a full-size base. A joint packed too tight holds water at the surface just as a bad rock base would.

What happens when a septic lid gets buried during a pool project

If a Windermere pool-area turf project doesn't keep a septic lid's location protected through a multi-day build, staged material or compacted base can end up covering it, and the state's rule requiring that access stay reachable doesn't help much once turf and infill are already finished on top of it. A pump-out crew arriving later without a clear record of the lid's exact spot sometimes has to probe through finished turf to find it, which damages a section that was otherwise built correctly. A marked stake through construction, not just a note on the layout plan, is what actually prevents this.

Confirming the drain point before infill goes down

Once the drainage underlay is glued to a Windermere lanai floor but before any infill goes in, the crew runs water across the surface to confirm it actually reaches the deck's existing drain rather than pooling in a low spot the underlay created by accident. Catching a flat or misdirected section at this stage means lifting a corner of underlay and reworking it, which is straightforward before infill is down and considerably more disruptive after. This check takes a few minutes and is the reason a finished lanai floor rarely surprises anyone with standing water months later.

Two reasons to rinse a pool border more than once a week in summer

Hosing down turf along a Windermere pool deck does two jobs at once: it clears chlorine or salt splash and pollen before either dries into the fibers, and it drops surface temperature 30 to 50 degrees ahead of an afternoon swim. Rainy-season storms between June and September handle some of that rinsing on their own, but the dry stretches on either side of summer leave splash as the only source of moisture on the turf, so a hose rinse earns its place in the routine year-round rather than just during the hottest weeks. Keeping shock and acid containers off the turf's edge avoids undoing the rinse entirely.

Low-E glass around a lake-view lanai

A lanai or pool cage with large low-emissivity windows facing it, common on newer lakefront construction that maximizes the water view, can reflect enough concentrated sun to soften a synthetic lawn several feet away, since the material starts to give in the 175 to 200°F range under that kind of focused heat. Checking which windows face the turf before installation is a cheaper step than repairing a scorched patch after the fact.

Low-emissivity glass near a pool cage isn't unique to this town either; it turns up on lake-view lots toward Winter Garden, Horizon West and Pine Hills just as often, and this piece on turf and reflected heat explains the mechanics behind it. The pool and lanai turf page covers the glue-down build in full.

Questions people ask

Can turf go all the way to the water on a Windermere lake lot?

Only if a seawall or bulkhead already separates the yard from the lake. Without one, the state's May 2026 standard keeps synthetic turf at least 10 feet from the ordinary or mean high water line, the same rule that applies to any Florida waterfront lot.

Does turf inside a screened lanai still need a drainage layer?

Yes, when it's going over existing concrete or pavers. A screen keeps rain out but not entirely, and any rinse water needs somewhere to go besides sitting on the slab, so a drainage underlay under the turf backing is standard for that setup.
